parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which activity is book-keeping rather than accounting?
A entering each day's credit sales in the sales journal
B comparing this year's profit with last year's profit
C deciding whether to open a second branch using the financial statements
D explaining to the owner why the gross margin has fallen
parts.answer: A entering each day's credit sales in the sales journal
parts.working: Book-keeping is the detailed recording of transactions in the books of prime entry and ledgers, so entering credit sales in the sales journal is book-keeping. Comparing profits (B), using statements for a decision (C) and explaining a ratio (D) are accounting: analysing, interpreting and communicating the information.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is NOT a purpose of measuring the profit or loss of a business?
A to help the owner decide how much can safely be taken as drawings
B to show whether the business is performing better than in the previous year
C to provide information when applying for a bank loan
D to record every transaction in a book of prime entry
parts.answer: D to record every transaction in a book of prime entry
parts.working: Recording transactions in books of prime entry is a book-keeping task, not a reason for measuring profit. A, B and C are all reasons why the profit figure is needed (drawings, monitoring progress, information for lenders).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statements about accounting are correct?
1 It summarises, analyses and interprets the financial records of a business.
2 It is concerned only with transactions paid in cash.
3 It provides information that helps the owner make decisions.
A 1 and 2 only
B 1 and 3 only
C 2 and 3 only
D 1, 2 and 3
parts.answer: B 1 and 3 only
parts.working: Statements 1 and 3 describe accounting. Statement 2 is wrong: credit transactions (credit sales, credit purchases, amounts owing) are recorded and summarised too, so any option that includes 2 is wrong.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Farah owns a stationery shop in Multan. Which item should NOT be recorded in the books of the shop?
A a cheque received from a school for exercise books supplied on credit last month
B the shop's electricity bill paid by bank transfer
C Farah's private house rent paid from her personal bank account
D stationery taken from the shop by Farah for her children
parts.answer: C Farah's private house rent paid from her personal bank account
parts.working: Only transactions that affect the business are recorded. Farah's house rent paid from her personal account does not involve the business at all. D must be recorded (as drawings), because business goods have left the business. A and B are ordinary business transactions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between book-keeping and accounting.
parts.answer: Book-keeping is the detailed recording of financial transactions in the books of the business; accounting uses those records to prepare, summarise, analyse and interpret financial statements.
parts.working: 1 mark: book-keeping = recording transactions (in books of prime entry/ledgers). 1 mark: accounting = summarising/analysing/interpreting/communicating the recorded information (e.g. preparing financial statements).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two reasons why a business owner needs to know the profit or loss of the business.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. to decide how much can be taken as drawings; to compare performance with earlier years; to support a loan application; to calculate tax; to decide whether to expand or close.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid reasons: drawings decision; monitoring progress/comparison with previous periods or other businesses; information for lenders/bank; tax assessment; planning decisions (expand, cut costs, close).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by profit.
parts.answer: Profit is the amount by which the income (revenue) of a period is greater than the expenses of that period.
parts.working: 1 mark: income/revenue exceeds expenses for the period.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what is meant by a loss.
parts.answer: A loss is the amount by which the expenses of a period are greater than the income of that period.
parts.working: 1 mark: expenses exceed income/revenue for the period.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the effect of (i) a profit and (ii) a loss on the owner's capital.
parts.answer: (i) A profit increases the owner's capital. (ii) A loss decreases the owner's capital.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Kwame runs a small printing business in Accra. Explain two ways in which accounting information helps him to monitor the progress of his business.
parts.answer: e.g. He can compare this year's profit with previous years to see whether the business is growing. He can compare actual expenses with what he planned, so he can see where costs are rising and take action.
parts.working: Two points × (1 mark for the point + 1 mark for development). Points: comparison of profit/revenue with earlier periods; comparison with budgets/targets; comparison with similar businesses; checking liquidity (cash/bank, amounts owed by customers); identifying expenses that are rising.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ali sells fresh juice from a stall in Lahore. In March his sales were $3,150. His expenses were: cost of fruit used $780, wages of a helper $900, stall rent $650 and electricity $210. Calculate Ali's profit for March.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Ali wants to take $900 from the business for his own use each month. Using your answer to (a), explain whether this is sensible.
parts.answer: Not sensible: $900 is more than the profit of $610, so his capital would fall by $290 each month if this continued.
parts.working: 1 mark: compares drawings with profit (drawings > profit). 1 mark: explains that capital/resources of the business would fall (own figure accepted).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Mehwish makes and sells cakes from her home in Islamabad. She keeps no records except her bank statements. She is thinking of keeping a full set of accounting records.
Advise Mehwish whether she should keep a full set of accounting records. Justify your answer by giving two points for and two points against.
parts.answer: For: she could calculate her profit accurately and know whether the business is worth continuing; records help control customers who owe money and suppliers she owes; she would have evidence for a bank loan or tax. Against: it takes time she could spend baking; she may need to pay a book-keeper or buy software; for a very small business the bank statement may give enough information. Recommendation: e.g. she should keep records, because the benefit of knowing her true profit outweighs the cost.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for points for (e.g. accurate profit; credit control; information for lenders/tax; separates business and private money; helps decisions such as pricing). Up to 2 marks for points against (time; cost of book-keeper/software; needs skill; small business may not need it). 1 mark for a clear recommendation supported by the points. Recommendation mark only if both sides are discussed.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each task, state whether it is book-keeping or accounting.
(i) Posting the totals of the purchases journal to the ledger.
(ii) Preparing an income statement for the year.
(iii) Writing up the petty cash book.
(iv) Calculating and commenting on the current ratio.
parts.answer: (i) book-keeping (ii) accounting (iii) book-keeping (iv) accounting

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a business that makes a profit for a year may still be short of money in its bank account.
parts.answer: Profit is not the same as cash. Some sales may be on credit and the money not yet received; cash may have been spent on non-current assets or used to repay loans; the owner may have taken large drawings. None of these reduces profit, but they reduce the bank balance.
parts.working: 1 mark: profit ≠ cash/bank. 1 mark each (max 2) for reasons: credit sales not yet received; purchase of non-current assets; drawings; loan repayments; increase in inventory; paying suppliers quickly.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Below is a list of payments and receipts of a delivery business owned by Tomás for April.
Cash from customers for deliveries $7,400
Fuel $1,350
Driver's wages $2,100
New delivery van $18,000 (paid by loan received from bank $18,000)
Insurance for April $240
Cash taken by Tomás for his own use $1,500
Van repairs $420
Ignore depreciation. Calculate Tomás's profit for April.
parts.working: Expenses = fuel 1,350 + wages 2,100 + insurance 240 + repairs 420 = 4,110 (M1). Van (capital expenditure), loan received and drawings are not income or expenses (M1 for excluding them). Profit = 7,400 − 4,110 = 3,290 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the cash taken by Tomás is not treated as an expense of the business.
parts.answer: It is drawings: money taken by the owner for private use. It was not spent to earn the business's income, so it reduces capital rather than profit.
parts.working: 1 mark: it is drawings/for private use. 1 mark: reduces capital, not an expense of earning revenue (business entity).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two reasons why a business keeps accounting records.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. to know how much is owed to and by the business; to calculate profit or loss; to know the value of assets; to provide information for tax or lenders; to help control the business.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid reasons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the name of the person who records the day-to-day transactions of a business.
parts.answer: A book-keeper.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ngozi owns a clothing shop in Lagos and is deciding whether to open a second shop. Explain two pieces of accounting information she should look at before deciding, and how each would help her.
parts.answer: e.g. Profit for recent years: rising profits suggest the business can support expansion. Bank balance/working capital: shows whether she can pay for fitting out a second shop or whether she will need a loan.
parts.working: Two × (1 mark information + 1 mark how it helps). Accept: profit trend; gross/profit margin; cash/bank balance; working capital; level of loans; expenses of the existing shop; forecast/budget figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Sana runs a tuition centre in Karachi. In January her fee income was $12,600 and her expenses were $9,450. In February her fee income was $14,100 and her expenses were $11,280. Calculate her profit for each month.
parts.answer: January $3,150; February $2,820

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in profit from January to February. Give your answer correct to two decimal places.
parts.answer: a fall of 10.48%

parts.label: c
parts.text: Sana's fee income rose. Explain why it is still important for her to measure profit every month.
parts.answer: Higher income does not always mean higher profit: her expenses rose faster than income, so profit fell. Measuring profit shows this early so she can control costs or change fees.
parts.working: 1 mark: income rising does not guarantee profit rising/expenses rose faster. 1 mark: allows early action (control costs, review fees, decisions).

parts.label: a
parts.text: In June, Rana's tailoring business had income of $25,400 and expenses of $27,150. Calculate the result for June and state whether it is a profit or a loss.
parts.answer: A loss of $1,750

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one decision that the owner of a business might make using accounting information.
parts.answer: e.g. whether to expand, whether to borrow, how much to take as drawings, whether to cut expenses, what prices to charge.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why accounting records must be accurate and kept up to date. Give two reasons.
parts.answer: e.g. Accurate records give a correct profit figure, so decisions such as drawings or expansion are based on true information. Up-to-date records show which customers owe money now, so they can be chased before the debts become irrecoverable.
parts.working: Two × (1 mark reason + 1 mark explanation). Reasons: correct profit/decisions; credit control; paying suppliers on time to keep discounts and goodwill; tax returns; lenders/investors rely on them; detecting fraud or errors quickly.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between income and capital introduced by the owner.
parts.answer: Income is earned by the business from its activities (e.g. sales, rent received) and increases profit. Capital introduced is money or assets put into the business by the owner; it increases capital but is not profit.
parts.working: 1 mark: income earned from trading/operations and included in profit. 1 mark: capital introduced is the owner's investment, not part of profit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Ravi paid $5,000 of his own savings into the business bank account and also received $2,300 rent from sub-letting part of the shop. State how much of the $7,300 is income of the business.
parts.working: 1 mark: only the rent received is income; the $5,000 is capital introduced.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hamid runs a computer repair business. He calculates his profit for the year as cash received $46,800 minus cash paid for expenses $39,200. Calculate the profit he has worked out.

parts.label: b
parts.text: At the end of the year customers owed Hamid $3,900 for repairs done during the year, and he owed $1,150 for electricity used during the year. There were no such amounts at the start of the year. Calculate the correct profit for the year.
parts.working: 7600 + 3900 (M1) − 1150 (M1) = 10350. Allow A1 for the final figure only if both adjustments are correct.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why Hamid's method does not measure profit correctly.
parts.answer: Profit should include all income earned and all expenses incurred in the year, whether or not cash has been received or paid. His method leaves out work done on credit and expenses owing.
parts.working: 1 mark: income/expenses must relate to the period (earned/incurred), not to cash movements. 1 mark: identifies credit income not received or expenses unpaid as the cause.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A business has assets of $48,000 and liabilities of $13,500. What is the owner's capital?
A $34,500
B $61,500
C $13,500
D $48,000
parts.working: Capital = assets − liabilities = 48000 − 13500 = 34500. B wrongly adds the liabilities to the assets.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A business buys inventory on credit. What is the effect on the accounting equation?
A assets increase and capital increases
B assets increase and liabilities increase
C assets decrease and liabilities increase
D no change in assets; liabilities increase
parts.answer: B assets increase and liabilities increase
parts.working: Inventory (an asset) increases and the amount owed to the supplier (a trade payable, a liability) increases by the same amount. Capital is unchanged because no income or expense has arisen, so A is wrong.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A business has total assets of $75,000 and total liabilities of $22,000. It then pays a supplier $4,000 by bank transfer and buys office equipment for $6,000 on credit. What are the total assets after these transactions?
A $85,000
B $81,000
C $77,000
D $71,000
parts.working: Paying the supplier: bank −4,000 and payables −4,000. Equipment on credit: assets +6,000 and liabilities +6,000. Assets = 75000 − 4,000 + 6,000 = 77000 (liabilities become 24000; capital stays 53000). B forgets to reduce the bank balance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the accounting equation.
parts.answer: Assets = Liabilities + Capital (owner's equity)

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Calculate the missing figure for each business.
(i) Assets $62,000; Liabilities $17,500; Capital ?
(ii) Assets ?; Liabilities $8,200; Capital $41,300
(iii) Assets $29,750; Liabilities ?; Capital $23,900

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State whether each item is an asset or a liability of a business.
(i) Delivery van
(ii) Bank loan repayable in five years
(iii) Amounts owed by credit customers
(iv) Amounts owed to suppliers
(v) Inventory of goods for resale
(vi) Bank overdraft
parts.answer: (i) asset (ii) liability (iii) asset (iv) liability (v) asset (vi) liability
parts.working: 1 mark for each two correct answers (6 correct = 3 marks).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a liability.
parts.answer: An amount owed by the business to someone outside the business (e.g. a supplier or lender).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each transaction, state the effect (increase, decrease or no effect) on total assets, total liabilities and capital.
(i) The owner pays $10,000 of personal money into the business bank account.
(ii) Goods for resale bought by cheque, $1,800.
(iii) A trade payable is paid $950 by bank transfer.
(iv) The owner takes $400 cash for private use.
(v) A bank loan of $6,000 is received.
parts.answer:
(i) assets increase, liabilities no effect, capital increase
(ii) no effect on total assets (inventory up, bank down), liabilities no effect, capital no effect
(iii) assets decrease, liabilities decrease, capital no effect
(iv) assets decrease, liabilities no effect, capital decrease
(v) assets increase, liabilities increase, capital no effect
parts.working: 1 mark for each transaction with all three effects correct.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Zainab's boutique had the following balances on 30 June:
Premises $85,000
Fixtures $12,400
Inventory $9,650
Trade receivables $4,300
Bank $2,780
Trade payables $6,120
Loan from Habib Bank (repayable in 2031) $30,000
Wages owing $540
Calculate (i) total assets, (ii) total liabilities and (iii) Zainab's capital on 30 June.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
On 1 May Chen started a business by paying $20,000 into a business bank account. During May:
1 bought equipment by cheque, $7,500
2 bought inventory on credit from Lee Traders, $3,200
3 received a bank loan, $5,000
4 sold goods that had cost $1,000 for $1,600 cash
Calculate the total assets, total liabilities and capital after transaction 4.
parts.answer: Assets $28,800; Liabilities $8,200; Capital $20,600

parts.label: a
parts.text: On 1 January Imran's capital was $54,300. During the year his business made a profit of $17,850, he took drawings of $11,200 and he paid in additional capital of $4,000. Calculate his capital on 31 December.

parts.label: b
parts.text: On 31 December the business's liabilities were $23,650. Calculate its total assets.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why drawings reduce the owner's capital but are not an expense.
parts.answer: Drawings are resources taken out by the owner for private use, so the owner's claim on the business falls. They are not used to earn income, so they are not charged in the income statement.
parts.working: 1 mark: capital = owner's claim, which is reduced by withdrawals. 1 mark: not incurred to earn revenue/business entity, so not an expense.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Precious owns a catering business in Nairobi. At the start of June the business had assets of $36,000 and liabilities of $9,000. During June:
1 Precious brought her own car, valued at $8,500, into the business.
2 The business received a loan of $12,000 from a finance company.
3 Precious took food that had cost the business $650 for a family wedding.
4 A supplier was paid $2,400 by bank transfer.
Calculate the total assets, total liabilities and capital at the end of June. Show your working.
parts.answer: Assets $53,450; Liabilities $18,600; Capital $34,850

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why transaction 4 does not change the capital.
parts.answer: Assets (bank) and liabilities (trade payables) both fall by $2,400, so assets − liabilities is unchanged.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by the owner's capital.
parts.answer: The amount the business owes to its owner: the owner's investment plus profits retained, less drawings (assets minus liabilities).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the accounting equation always balances after every transaction.
parts.answer: Every transaction has two equal effects (duality), e.g. an asset increases and another asset decreases, or an asset and a liability both increase, so assets always equal liabilities plus capital.
parts.working: 1 mark: every transaction has two aspects/duality. 1 mark: the two effects are equal, so both sides change by the same amount (or example).

subtopic: Correction of errors and suspense accounts

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A credit sale of $350 to Raza Traders was correctly entered in the sales journal but was posted to the account of Rehman Traders. What type of error is this?
A commission
B principle
C original entry
D omission
parts.answer: A commission
parts.working: The amount is posted to the wrong account of the same class (the wrong customer's account), which is an error of commission. It is not an error of principle, because both accounts are personal accounts of credit customers.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Correction of errors and suspense accounts

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which error will cause the totals of a trial balance to disagree?
A a credit sale of $800 was omitted from the books completely
B the purchase of a computer for office use was debited to the purchases account
C discount allowed of $50 was entered in the discount allowed account but not in the customer's account
D a payment received from Ali was credited to Ahmed's account
parts.answer: C discount allowed of $50 was entered in the discount allowed account but not in the customer's account
parts.working: In C only one side of the double entry was made (a debit with no matching credit), so the trial balance will not agree. A (omission), B (principle) and D (commission) all have equal debits and credits, so the trial balance still agrees.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Correction of errors and suspense accounts

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The purchase of an office printer costing $900 was debited to the purchases account. Depreciation is ignored. What is the effect of this error?
A gross profit and profit for the year are both understated by $900
B gross profit is understated by $900 but profit for the year is not affected
C gross profit and profit for the year are both overstated by $900
D profit for the year is not affected but non-current assets are overstated by $900
parts.answer: A gross profit and profit for the year are both understated by $900
parts.working: Purchases are overstated by $900, so cost of sales is $900 too high, and gross profit and therefore profit are both $900 too low. B is wrong because a lower gross profit carries through to profit. Non-current assets are understated, not overstated.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Correction of errors and suspense accounts

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A trader's draft profit for the year was $23,400. Two errors were then found:
1 discount received of $150 had been debited to the discount allowed account
2 closing inventory had been overstated by $1,200
What is the corrected profit for the year?
A $22,500
B $22,350
C $24,900
D $21,900
parts.working: Error 1: an expense (discount allowed) is overstated by $150 and income (discount received) is understated by $150, so profit is $300 too low: +300. Error 2: overstated closing inventory makes profit too high: −1,200. 23400 + 300 − 1,200 = 22500. B adjusts error 1 by only $150.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Correction of errors and suspense accounts

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the type of error in each case.
(i) A payment of $260 for electricity was not recorded in the books at all.
(ii) The purchase of a delivery van was debited to the motor expenses account.
(iii) A credit sale of $1,470 was entered in the sales journal as $1,740 and posted from there.
(iv) A cheque paid to a supplier was debited to the bank account and credited to the supplier's account.
parts.answer: (i) omission (ii) principle (iii) original entry (iv) complete reversal

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Correction of errors and suspense accounts

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two types of error that are not revealed by a trial balance.
parts.answer: Any two of: omission, commission, principle, original entry, complete reversal, compensating errors.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a suspense account may be opened when a trial balance is prepared.
parts.answer: When the trial balance totals do not agree, the difference is entered in a suspense account so that the totals agree temporarily and the financial statements can be drafted until the errors are found and corrected.
parts.working: 1 mark: totals disagree/difference recorded. 1 mark: temporary account until errors are found and corrected.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Correction of errors and suspense accounts

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Prepare journal entries to correct the following errors. Narratives are not required.
(i) Repairs to machinery, $640, were debited to the machinery account.
(ii) A credit sale of $1,230 to Lim Hardware was entered in the books as $1,320.
(iii) A payment of $500 by cheque to Patel Supplies was debited to the bank account and credited to Patel Supplies' account.
parts.answer:
(i) Dr Machinery repairs $640; Cr Machinery $640
(ii) Dr Sales $90; Cr Lim Hardware $90
(iii) Dr Patel Supplies $1,000; Cr Bank $1,000
parts.working: 2 marks per entry (1 debit, 1 credit with correct amount). (ii) difference 1,320 − 1,230 = 90. (iii) complete reversal is corrected with twice the amount: 2 × 500 = 1,000.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Correction of errors and suspense accounts

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Shabnam's trial balance on 31 December had debit totals of $61,250 and credit totals of $61,650. The difference was entered in a suspense account. These errors were then found:
1 The purchases journal had been undercast by $280.
2 Rent paid of $1,150 had been entered in the rent account as $1,050.
3 Cash sales of $490 had been credited to the sales account as $510.
Prepare the suspense account, showing the opening balance and the corrections.
parts.answer: Suspense account: Dr balance b/d $400. Cr Purchases $280, Cr Rent $100, Cr Sales $20. Totals $400 each side.
parts.working: Opening balance: credits exceed debits by 61,650 − 61,250 = 400, so suspense has a debit balance of $400 (1). Purchases 280 on credit side (1). Rent 1,150 − 1,050 = 100 on credit side (1). Sales 510 − 490 = 20 on credit side (1); account closes with 280 + 100 + 20 = 400.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one error that would not be corrected through the suspense account.
parts.answer: e.g. an error of omission, commission, principle, original entry, complete reversal or compensating error (with example).

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Correction of errors and suspense accounts

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each error state whether the profit for the year is overstated, understated or not affected, and by how much.
(i) Closing inventory was undervalued by $500.
(ii) Rent received of $300 was credited to the commission received account.
(iii) The purchase of shop fixtures, $750, was debited to the repairs account.
(iv) Wages owing of $420 at the year end were not recorded.
(v) A credit sale of $600 was omitted from the books.
parts.answer: (i) understated $500 (ii) not affected (iii) understated $750 (iv) overstated $420 (v) understated $600
parts.working: 1 mark each. (ii) both accounts are income accounts, so total income is unchanged. (iii) capital expenditure treated as an expense. (iv) an expense is missing.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Correction of errors and suspense accounts
stem:
Kofi's trial balance on 31 March did not agree: the debit side totalled $86,420 and the credit side $85,950. The difference was entered in a suspense account and a draft profit for the year of $18,600 was calculated. The following errors were then found:
1 The sales journal had been undercast by $300.
2 Wages of $1,240 had been entered in the wages account as $1,420.
3 Rent received of $250 had been entered in the bank account but omitted from the rent received account.
4 Discount allowed of $85 had not been posted to the discount allowed account.
5 A payment of $175 to Chen, a supplier, had been entered correctly in the cash book but not posted to Chen's account.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the suspense account, starting with the balance arising from the trial balance.
parts.answer: Suspense: Cr balance b/d $470. Dr Sales $300, Dr Wages $180, Dr Rent received $250. Cr Discount allowed $85, Cr Chen $175. Totals $730 each side.
parts.working: Opening: debits exceed credits by 86420 − 85950 = 470, so a credit balance of 470 (1). Debit entries 300, 180 (1,420 − 1,240), 250 (1). Credit entries 85 and 175 (1). Both sides total 730.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prepare a statement showing the corrected profit for the year.
parts.working: Draft 18,600 + sales 300 (1) + wages 180 (1) + rent received 250 (1) − discount allowed 85 (1) = 19245. Error 5 affects only Chen's account and the suspense account, so there is no effect on profit.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Correction of errors and suspense accounts

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by an error of principle.
parts.answer: An amount is entered in the correct amount and on the correct side, but in the wrong class of account, e.g. capital expenditure entered in an expense account.
parts.working: 1 mark: wrong class/type of account. 1 mark: example, e.g. purchase of a non-current asset debited to an expense account.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether an error of principle will cause the trial balance totals to disagree. Give a reason.
parts.answer: No. The debit and the credit entries are still equal, so the totals agree.
parts.working: 1 mark: no. 1 mark: reason (equal debit and credit).

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Correction of errors and suspense accounts

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Rosa's draft profit for the year ended 30 September was $31,560. The following errors were found:
1 Carriage outwards of $240, paid in cash, had not been recorded.
2 Discount allowed of $160 had been credited to the discount received account.
3 The purchase of office equipment, $1,200, had been debited to the office expenses account.
4 Closing inventory had been overstated by $700.
Prepare a statement of corrected profit for the year. Depreciation is ignored.
parts.working: Draft 31560 − 240 (1) − 320 (1: income overstated 160 and expense understated 160) + 1,200 (1) − 700 (1) = 31500 (1 for final figure with correct method).

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Correction of errors and suspense accounts
stem:
Bilal's draft financial statements for the year ended 31 December showed a profit of $27,400 and total current assets of $18,900. The following matters had not been dealt with:
1 Insurance of $360 had been paid in advance for next year.
2 A trade receivable of $520 was known to be irrecoverable and should be written off.
3 Closing inventory included goods that cost $900 but could only be sold for $650.
4 Commission of $430 was receivable but had not been received or recorded.
5 Cash drawings of $600 had been debited to the wages account.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit for the year.
parts.working: 27400 + 360 − 520 − 250 (900 − 650) + 430 + 600 = 28020. 1 mark for each two correct adjustments (max 3), 1 for the final figure.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the corrected total current assets.
parts.working: 18900 + 360 prepayment − 520 receivable − 250 inventory + 430 commission receivable = 18920. Item 5 does not affect current assets. 2 marks for adjustments, 1 for the final figure.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A credit purchase of $2,100 from Bilal Traders was completely omitted from the books. Prepare the journal entry to correct this error. A narrative is not required.
parts.answer: Dr Purchases $2,100; Cr Bilal Traders $2,100

parts.label: b

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Correction of errors and suspense accounts

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a compensating error.
parts.answer: Two or more separate errors that cancel each other out, e.g. the sales account overcast by $100 and the wages account overcast by $100.
parts.working: 1 mark: two errors cancelling each other. 1 mark: example or statement that the trial balance still agrees.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A credit sale of $745 to Kim was entered in the sales journal as $475 and posted from there. Prepare the journal entry to correct this error. A narrative is not required.

parts.text: State the name of this type of error.
parts.answer: Error of original entry

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Correction of errors and suspense accounts
stem:
After a suspense account was opened, the following errors were found in Olena's books:
1 Discount received of $230 had not been posted to the discount received account.
2 The total of the sales returns journal, $410, had been posted to the credit of the sales returns account.
3 A cheque for $1,500 received from Fatima, a customer, had been entered correctly in the bank account but credited to Fatima's account as $1,050.
No other errors were found and correcting them closed the suspense account.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare the journal entries to correct these errors. Narratives are not required.
parts.answer:
1 Dr Suspense $230; Cr Discount received $230
2 Dr Sales returns $820; Cr Suspense $820
3 Dr Suspense $450; Cr Fatima $450
parts.working: 2 marks each. Error 2: the amount was entered on the wrong side, so twice the amount (2 × 410 = 820) is needed. Error 3: 1,500 − 1,050 = 450.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the balance in the suspense account before the corrections were made and state whether it was a debit or a credit balance.
parts.answer: Debit balance of $140
parts.working: Corrections: debits to suspense 230 + 450 = 680; credit to suspense 820. For the account to close, the opening balance must be a debit of 820 − 680 = 140 (1 amount, 1 side).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A trader's updated cash book shows a debit balance of $2,340. Cheques paid to suppliers of $610 have not yet been presented, and a deposit of $450 has not yet been credited by the bank. What balance is shown on the bank statement?
A $2,500
B $2,180
C $3,400
D $1,280
parts.working: Unpresented cheques have not yet left the bank account, so the bank balance is higher: +610. The deposit is not yet on the statement, so the bank balance is lower: −450. 2340 + 610 − 450 = 2500. B reverses both adjustments.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two reasons why the balance in the cash book may differ from the balance on the bank statement on the same date.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. unpresented cheques; amounts paid in but not yet credited; bank charges or interest not yet entered in the cash book; standing orders or direct debits not yet recorded; credit transfers not yet recorded; dishonoured cheques; errors.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is meant by an unpresented cheque.
parts.answer: A cheque that has been written and entered in the cash book but has not yet been paid by the bank (not yet on the bank statement).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
On 31 August the bank column of Yasmin's cash book showed a debit balance of $3,870. Her bank statement showed these items that were not in the cash book:
• bank charges, $45
• direct debit for insurance, $220
• credit transfer received from a customer, $680
• a cheque for $350 received from Ahmed had been dishonoured
State which of these items should be entered on the debit side of the cash book.
parts.answer: Only the credit transfer of $680.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the updated cash book balance on 31 August.
parts.answer: $3,935 debit
parts.working: 3,870 + 680 − 45 − 220 − 350 = 3935. 1 mark for adding 680, 1 for deducting the three payments, 1 for the final figure.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
After updating, the cash book of Hassan Electricals showed a debit balance of $5,612 on 30 June. The bank statement balance on the same date was $6,327. The difference was caused by:
• cheques paid to suppliers but not yet presented: $1,380 and $455
• cash paid in on 30 June but not yet credited by the bank: $1,120
Prepare a bank reconciliation statement on 30 June, starting with the balance on the bank statement.
parts.answer: Balance per bank statement $6,327; add amount not credited $1,120; less unpresented cheques $1,835; balance per cash book $5,612.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name one item that would be entered in the cash book when it is updated but would not appear in the bank reconciliation statement.
parts.answer: e.g. bank charges, a standing order, a direct debit, a credit transfer, interest or a dishonoured cheque.

stem:
On 31 October the bank column of Soo-jin's cash book showed an overdraft of $1,460. Comparison with the bank statement showed:
1 A standing order of $300 for rent had been paid by the bank but not entered in the cash book.
2 Bank interest of $85 had been charged.
3 A customer had paid $540 by credit transfer.
4 A cheque for $910 sent to a supplier had not been presented.
5 Takings of $1,275 paid in on 31 October had not been credited by the bank.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the updated cash book balance on 31 October. State whether it is a debit or a credit balance.
parts.answer: $1,305 credit (overdraft)
parts.working: −1,460 − 300 − 85 + 540 = -1305 (2 marks for adjustments), so an overdraft of 1305, a credit balance (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the balance shown on the bank statement on 31 October, stating whether it is an overdraft.
parts.answer: Overdraft of $1,670
parts.working: -1305 + 910 unpresented (1) − 1,275 not credited (1) = -1670, an overdraft of 1670 (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State where the updated cash book balance will appear in the statement of financial position.
parts.answer: Under current liabilities (bank overdraft).

stem:
On 31 May the bank statement of Dario's shop showed a balance of $8,140 in his favour. The following information is available:
• cheques of $2,350 entered in the cash book had not been presented

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the updated cash book balance on 31 May.

parts.label: b

parts.text: State two benefits to Dario of preparing a bank reconciliation statement regularly.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. errors in the cash book or by the bank are found quickly; fraud is more likely to be detected; it shows which cheques are still unpresented or dishonoured; the cash book balance is brought up to date for the financial statements.
parts.working: 1 mark each. Do not accept vague answers such as 'finds errors' without saying where.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which item is entered on the credit side of a sales ledger control account?
A credit sales for the month
B cheques received from credit customers
C a customer's cheque that has been dishonoured
D the balance owed by customers brought down
parts.answer: B cheques received from credit customers
parts.working: Money received from credit customers reduces the amount they owe, so it is credited. Credit sales, dishonoured cheques and the opening debit balance all increase the amount owed and are debited.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two benefits of keeping control accounts.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. they check the arithmetical accuracy of the sales or purchases ledger; they help locate errors in a particular ledger; they give a quick total of trade receivables or payables; they help prevent fraud because the control account can be kept by a different person.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the source of information for (i) credit sales and (ii) discount allowed in a sales ledger control account.
parts.answer: (i) sales journal (ii) discount allowed column of the cash book

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Prepare the sales ledger control account of Mirza Wholesale for March from the following information.
Balance owed by customers on 1 March $14,620
Credit sales $38,450
Sales returns $1,270
Cheques received from customers $35,900
Discount allowed $640
Irrecoverable debts written off $410
Customer's cheque dishonoured $300
Balance the account on 31 March and bring down the balance on 1 April.
parts.answer: Debit side: balance b/d 14,620, sales 38,450, bank (dishonoured cheque) 300 = 53,370. Credit side: sales returns 1,270, bank 35,900, discount allowed 640, irrecoverable debts 410, balance c/d 15,150. Balance b/d on 1 April $15,150 debit.
parts.working: 1 mark for the debit entries, 1 for returns and bank, 1 for discount and irrecoverable debts, 1 for balance c/d 15,150, 1 for balance b/d on the debit side.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The following information relates to the purchases ledger of Kaur Fabrics for April.
Balance owed to suppliers on 1 April $9,840
Credit purchases $27,300
Payments to suppliers $25,150
Discount received $520
Purchases returns $860
Amount set off against the sales ledger (contra) $700
Calculate the balance on the purchases ledger control account on 30 April and state whether it is a debit or a credit balance.
parts.answer: $9,910 credit

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a contra entry (set-off) between the control accounts.
parts.answer: When a business both buys from and sells to the same firm, the amount the firm owes is set off against the amount owed to it, so only the net amount is paid. It is debited in the purchases ledger control account and credited in the sales ledger control account.
parts.working: 1 mark: same person is both customer and supplier and balances are set off. 1 mark: correct entries (Dr PLCA, Cr SLCA).

stem:
Yuki does not record credit sales in a sales journal. For the year ended 31 December she has the following information:
Trade receivables 1 January $12,300
Trade receivables 31 December $13,850
Cash and cheques received from credit customers $61,200
Discount allowed $1,150
Irrecoverable debts written off $600
Sales returns $2,050

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Yuki's credit sales for the year.
parts.working: Credit sales = closing 13,850 + receipts 61,200 + discount 1,150 + irrecoverable debts 600 + returns 2,050 − opening 12,300 = 66550. 3 marks for correct use of the items, 1 for the answer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The total of the balances in Yuki's sales ledger on 31 December was $13,530. Suggest two reasons why this total differs from the control account balance.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. a customer's balance has been omitted from the list; an item was posted to the control account but not to a customer's account (or the reverse); a customer's account was miscast; an item was posted to the wrong side of a customer's account.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how a sales ledger control account helps the owner to locate errors.
parts.answer: If the control account balance agrees with the total of the sales ledger balances, the ledger is probably arithmetically correct; if not, the error is in the sales ledger, so the search is limited to that ledger.
parts.working: 1 mark: comparison of control balance with list of balances. 1 mark: narrows the search to one ledger.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which balance appears on the credit side of a trial balance?
A drawings
B trade payables
C carriage inwards
D trade receivables
parts.answer: B trade payables
parts.working: Trade payables are a liability and have a credit balance. Drawings, carriage inwards (an expense) and trade receivables (an asset) have debit balances.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The following balances were taken from the books of Aryan Traders on 31 December.
Premises $60,000

Trade payables $5,750

Loan (repayable 2032) $20,000

Capital ?
Calculate the debit total of the trial balance and the capital balance that makes the trial balance agree.
parts.answer: Debit total $159,950; capital $55,850 (credit)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two limitations of a trial balance.
parts.answer: Any two: it does not reveal errors of omission, commission, principle, original entry, complete reversal or compensating errors; it only proves arithmetical accuracy of the double entry; it does not show profit.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Aziz and Bano share profits and losses in the ratio 3:2. Their profit for the year was $48,000. Interest on capital: Aziz $3,000, Bano $2,000. Bano receives a salary of $10,000. Interest on drawings: Aziz $500, Bano $300. What is Aziz's share of the residual profit?
A $20,280
B $19,800
C $28,800
D $13,520
parts.working: Residual profit = 48,000 + interest on drawings 800 − interest on capital 5,000 − salary 10,000 = 33800. Aziz's share = 3/5 × 33800 = 20280. B forgets to add interest on drawings; D is Bano's share.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two advantages of forming a partnership rather than continuing as a sole trader.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. more capital is available; partners bring different skills and ideas; work and responsibility are shared; losses are shared; cover during illness or holidays.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two disadvantages of forming a partnership rather than continuing as a sole trader.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. profits have to be shared; decisions take longer and partners may disagree; each partner is liable for the debts of the firm (unlimited liability); a partner is bound by the actions of the others.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State four items that are usually included in a partnership agreement.
parts.answer: Any four: the ratio for sharing profits and losses; capital to be contributed by each partner; interest on capital (rate); interest on drawings (rate); partners' salaries; limits on drawings; procedure for admitting or retiring partners; how disputes are settled.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the purpose of a partnership appropriation account.
parts.answer: It shows how the profit for the year is shared between the partners: interest on capital, salaries, interest on drawings and the share of the residual profit.
parts.working: 1 mark: shows how profit is divided/appropriated. 1 mark: names at least two items.

stem:

• drawings: Lerato $24,000, Sipho $18,500

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the balance on each partner's current account on 31 December. State whether each is a debit or a credit balance.
parts.answer: Lerato $3,220 debit; Sipho $1,370 credit

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what a debit balance on a partner's current account shows.
parts.answer: The partner has withdrawn more (drawings and interest on drawings) than the total of his or her share of profit, interest and salary, so the partner owes this amount to the business.
parts.working: 1 mark: drawings exceed amounts credited. 1 mark: partner owes the firm/reduces the partner's equity.

stem: Amina and Bashir share residual profits and losses in the ratio 2:1. The partnership agreement provides for interest on drawings at 10% per annum and a salary for Amina of $7,500 per year. No interest is allowed on capital. The financial year ends on 31 December. Amina withdrew $6,000 on 1 April and Bashir withdrew $8,000 on 1 October; there were no other drawings. The profit for the year was $39,100.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the interest on drawings for each partner.
parts.answer: Amina $450; Bashir $200
parts.working: Amina: 6,000 × 10% × 9/12 = 450 (1). Bashir: 8,000 × 10% × 3/12 = 200 (1). Charging a full year loses the mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate each partner's share of the residual profit.
parts.answer: Amina $21,500; Bashir $10,750

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a partnership agreement may charge interest on drawings.
parts.answer: To discourage partners from taking drawings early or in large amounts, which would reduce the cash available to the business.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A trader does not keep a full set of records. Her capital was $42,000 at the start of the year and $51,500 at the end. During the year her drawings were $12,000 and she introduced additional capital of $3,000. What was her profit for the year?
A $18,500
B $24,500
C $9,500
D $500
parts.working: Profit = closing capital + drawings − capital introduced − opening capital = 51,500 + 12,000 − 3,000 − 42,000 = 18500. B adds the capital introduced instead of deducting it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a statement of affairs.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A manufacturer provides the following information.
Inventory of raw materials: opening $4,200; closing $5,100
Purchases of raw materials $36,500
Carriage inwards on raw materials $800
Direct labour $28,000
Royalties $2,500
Factory rent $9,000
What is the prime cost?
A $66,900
B $66,100
C $64,400
D $68,700
parts.working: Raw materials consumed = 4,200 + 36,500 + 800 − 5,100 = 36400. Prime cost = 36400 + 28,000 + 2,500 = 66900. Factory rent is a factory overhead, not part of prime cost. B leaves out carriage inwards.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by prime cost.
parts.answer: The total of the direct costs of production: direct materials, direct labour and direct expenses (such as royalties).

parts.label: b
parts.text:
State where each cost appears: in the prime cost section of the manufacturing account, in factory overheads, or in the income statement.
(i) wages of machine operators
(ii) rent of the factory
(iii) commission paid to salespeople
(iv) depreciation of factory machinery
(v) salaries of office staff
(vi) raw materials used

parts.text: State how opening and closing work in progress are used to calculate the cost of production.
parts.answer: Opening work in progress is added to (and closing work in progress deducted from) the total of prime cost and factory overheads.
parts.working: 1 mark opening added, 1 mark closing deducted.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two reasons why a manufacturing business prepares a manufacturing account.
parts.answer: Any two: to calculate the cost of production of goods completed; to find the cost per unit; to control and compare factory costs; to help set selling prices; to decide whether to make or buy.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is meant by limited liability for the shareholders of a company?

B shareholders can lose only the amount they have invested in their shares
C shareholders receive a fixed dividend every year
D the company has a limited number of shareholders
parts.answer: B shareholders can lose only the amount they have invested in their shares
parts.working: With limited liability, shareholders' personal possessions cannot be used to pay the company's debts; the most they can lose is the amount paid for their shares. C describes a feature that ordinary shares do not have: ordinary dividends vary.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two differences between ordinary shares and debentures.
parts.answer: Ordinary shareholders are owners of the company, while debenture holders are lenders (creditors). Ordinary shareholders receive dividends that vary with profit and are paid only if declared; debenture holders receive a fixed rate of interest that must be paid whether or not there is a profit. (Also: shareholders usually have voting rights; debentures are repayable on a fixed date.)
parts.working: Two differences × 2 marks (1 for each side of the comparison).

stem:
On 1 January the equity of Indus Foods Ltd was: ordinary shares of $1 each $200,000; general reserve $30,000; retained earnings $47,500. During the year ended 31 December:

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the name of the financial statement in which these movements are shown.

stem: Kestrel Engineering Ltd has 6% debentures of $120,000, repayable in 2034. For the year ended 31 December the company's profit from operations was $84,600. Only $3,600 of debenture interest had been paid and recorded during the year. Retained earnings on 1 January were $52,300. During the year ordinary dividends of $30,000 were paid and $10,000 was transferred to the general reserve.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Mariam owns a successful bakery as a sole trader. She plans to form a limited company and issue 60,000 ordinary shares of $0.50 each at par. Calculate the amount the company would receive if all the shares were issued and fully paid.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise Mariam whether she should convert her business into a limited company. Justify your answer by giving two advantages and two disadvantages.
parts.answer: Advantages: limited liability protects her personal assets; more capital can be raised by selling shares; the company continues even if a shareholder dies or leaves. Disadvantages: she must share profits (dividends) and control with other shareholders; more legal formalities and costs; financial statements may have to be published, so there is less privacy. Recommendation, e.g. convert if she needs large amounts of capital for expansion; otherwise remain a sole trader.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks advantages, up to 2 marks disadvantages, 1 mark for a justified recommendation (only if both sides are given).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A tennis club received subscriptions of $8,400 during the year. This included $200 owing from the previous year and $600 paid in advance for next year. At the start of the year $300 had been paid in advance for this year. At the end of the year $450 was owing for this year. What is the subscriptions income for the year?
A $8,350
B $8,450
C $8,250
D $9,150
parts.working: 8,400 − 200 (last year's arrears) − 600 (next year) + 300 (paid last year for this year) + 450 (owing) = 8350. C ignores the opening balances.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In the financial statements of a club, the accumulated fund is equivalent to which item in the financial statements of a sole trader?
A capital
B profit for the year
C drawings
D bank balance
parts.answer: A capital
parts.working: The accumulated fund is the members' interest in the club: assets less liabilities, the same as a sole trader's capital. The surplus for the year (not the fund itself) corresponds to profit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two differences between a receipts and payments account and an income and expenditure account.
parts.answer: Any two: a receipts and payments account is a summary of the cash book, while an income and expenditure account is like an income statement; the receipts and payments account includes capital items, the income and expenditure account includes only revenue items; the income and expenditure account includes accruals, prepayments and depreciation, the receipts and payments account does not; the receipts and payments account ends with a cash/bank balance, the income and expenditure account with a surplus or deficit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The Gulberg Chess Club had the following subscription balances: 1 January: in arrears $240, in advance $180. 31 December: in arrears $510. During the year $9,850 was received, which included the $240 arrears from last year and $360 for next year. Calculate the subscriptions income for the year.
parts.working: 9,850 − 240 − 360 + 180 + 510 = 9940. 1 mark for removing the two amounts not for this year, 1 for adding 180 and 510, 1 for the answer.

stem:
The Riverside Hiking Society runs a small café for members. For the year ended 31 December:
Café takings $14,600; café purchases $8,900; café inventory 1 January $650, 31 December $820; café wages $3,100
Subscriptions income $12,400
Competition entry fees $1,350; competition prizes $980
Rent of clubhouse $6,000
Electricity paid $1,780; $160 was owing at 31 December (nothing owing at 1 January)
Depreciation of equipment $1,500

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit made by the café.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the surplus or deficit for the year.
parts.answer: Surplus of $6,100
parts.working: Income: 12,400 + café 2770 + net competition 370 = 15540 (2). Expenditure: 6,000 + electricity 1940 + 1,500 = 9440 (1). Surplus 6100 (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the effect of the surplus on the accumulated fund.
parts.answer: It increases the accumulated fund.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A trader provides this information: opening inventory $7,300; purchases $52,600; carriage inwards $900; purchases returns $1,400; closing inventory $8,100. What is the cost of sales?
A $51,300
B $50,400
C $54,100

stem:
The following information relates to Ewan's shop on 31 December, after the income statement had been prepared:
Premises $90,000
Fixtures at cost $18,000; accumulated depreciation $7,200

Trade receivables $8,400; provision for doubtful debts $420
Insurance prepaid $250

parts.label: b

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The owner of a pharmacy paid her personal mobile phone bill from the business bank account. The amount was recorded as drawings, not as an expense of the business. Which principle has been applied?
A business entity
B going concern
C realisation
D consistency
parts.answer: A business entity
parts.working: Business entity treats the business as separate from its owner, so the owner's private expense is drawings. Going concern (B) is about the business continuing in the future and is not relevant here.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Inventory is valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value. Which principle does this apply?
A matching
B prudence
C duality
D money measurement
parts.answer: B prudence
parts.working: Prudence means profits and assets are not overstated: if goods are expected to sell for less than cost, the loss is recognised now. Matching (A) concerns charging expenses to the period in which the related revenue is earned.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A business paid rent for 13 months during its financial year. Only 12 months' rent was charged in the income statement and the remainder was shown as a prepayment. Which principle has been applied?
A prudence
B consistency
C matching
D going concern
parts.answer: C matching
parts.working: Matching (accruals) requires expenses to be charged to the period to which they relate, whatever the date of payment, so one month is carried forward as a prepayment. Prudence (A) is about not overstating profit or assets.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which principle requires non-current assets to be recorded in the books at the price paid for them?
A historic cost
B materiality
C realisation
D money measurement
parts.answer: A historic cost
parts.working: Under historic cost, assets are recorded at their original cost, which can be checked against invoices. Money measurement (D) says only items that can be expressed in money are recorded, but does not say which money value is used.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statements about the going concern principle are correct?
1 It assumes the business will continue to operate for the foreseeable future.
2 If a business is about to close, its assets should be valued at the amounts they are expected to raise when sold.
3 It requires a business to make a profit every year.
A 1 and 2 only
B 1 and 3 only
C 2 and 3 only
D 1, 2 and 3
parts.answer: A 1 and 2 only
parts.working: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: a continuing business values non-current assets at cost less depreciation, but a business that is closing uses expected sale values. Statement 3 is wrong: a business can make a loss and still be a going concern.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the accounting principle applied in each case.
(i) A sale is recorded when the goods are delivered to the customer, not when the order is received.
(ii) A stapler costing $6 that will last several years is recorded as an expense.
(iii) Every transaction is recorded by a debit entry and a credit entry.
(iv) Machinery is shown at cost less depreciation because the business is expected to continue trading.
parts.answer: (i) realisation (ii) materiality (iii) duality (iv) going concern

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the money measurement principle.
parts.answer: Only transactions and items that can be expressed in money terms are recorded in the accounting records.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one example of something that is valuable to a business but is not recorded in its books because of this principle.
parts.answer: e.g. the skill or loyalty of the staff; good relations with customers; the owner's experience; a good location.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the duality principle.
parts.answer: Every transaction has two aspects, which are recorded as a debit entry in one account and an equal credit entry in another account.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Mustafa bought a computer for his business and paid $1,350 by cheque. State the two accounts affected and whether each is debited or credited.
parts.answer: Debit computer (office equipment) account $1,350; credit bank account $1,350.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the consistency principle.
parts.answer: Once a business has chosen an accounting method (e.g. a depreciation method), it should use the same method from one year to the next.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the consistency principle is important to users of financial statements.
parts.answer: It makes the results of different years comparable, so changes in profit reflect performance rather than a change of method.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the realisation principle.
parts.answer: Revenue is recognised (and profit is earned) when the goods or services are passed to the customer and the customer accepts liability to pay, not when cash is received or an order is made.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Goods were delivered to a customer on 29 December and the customer paid on 12 January. The business's year ends on 31 December. State in which year the sale should be recorded and give a reason.
parts.answer: In the year ending 31 December (the year of delivery), because the goods were delivered and the customer became liable to pay before the year end.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the materiality principle.
parts.answer: Items of small value need not be treated strictly according to the rules if this would not affect users' understanding; for example, a cheap item that will last several years can be treated as an expense.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A large supermarket chain bought a waste-paper bin for $9. Explain how it should be treated in the accounts and why.
parts.answer: Charge it as an expense in the income statement (not as a non-current asset), because the amount is too small to matter to users and depreciating it would waste time.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the business entity principle.
parts.answer: The business is treated as a separate entity from its owner, so only business transactions are recorded in the business's books.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Sadia took $250 of goods from her shop for her family. Explain how the business entity principle affects the recording of this transaction.
parts.answer: The goods are no longer a business asset used to earn revenue; they are recorded as drawings (debit drawings, credit purchases), reducing Sadia's capital rather than being treated as a business expense.
parts.working: 1 mark: drawings/not a business expense. 1 mark: correct entries or effect on capital.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Femi's financial year ends on 31 December. On 1 April he paid insurance of $4,500 covering the 15 months from 1 April to 30 June of the following year. Calculate the insurance expense for the year ended 31 December.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the amount that will be shown as a prepayment in the statement of financial position on 31 December.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the accounting principle applied.
parts.answer: Matching (accruals)

stem:
Lina sells kitchen appliances. At the year end she has three types of item in inventory:
Toasters: cost $1,200; net realisable value $1,500
Kettles: cost $860; net realisable value $610

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the value of Lina's closing inventory.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the accounting principle that requires inventory to be valued in this way.
parts.answer: Prudence

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate by how much profit would be overstated if all the inventory were valued at net realisable value.

stem:
Rashid Electronics has a financial year ending on 31 December. The following transactions took place in December:
1 Goods invoiced at $3,400 were delivered to a customer on 28 December; payment was received on 10 January.
2 A customer paid a deposit of $1,000 on 15 December for a television to be delivered on 5 January.
3 An order for goods worth $2,600 was received on 30 December; delivery is planned for February.
4 Cash sales for December were $5,800.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the revenue from these transactions that should be included for the year ended 31 December.
parts.working: Items 1 and 4 only: 3,400 + 5,800 = 9200. 1 mark each for including 1 and 4, 1 for excluding 2 and 3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the deposit in transaction 2 is not revenue for the year ended 31 December.
parts.answer: The goods have not yet been delivered, so the sale has not been realised. The deposit is money owed back to the customer (a liability) until the television is delivered.
parts.working: 1 mark: not realised/goods not delivered. 1 mark: treated as a liability/deferred income.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Tariq bought a machine for $40,000. He could depreciate it by the straight-line method over 10 years with no residual value, or by the reducing balance method at 25% per annum. Calculate the depreciation charge for the first year under each method.
parts.answer: Straight-line $4,000; reducing balance $10,000

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the effect on the profit for the first year of using the reducing balance method instead of the straight-line method.
parts.answer: Profit is $6,000 lower.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Tariq suggests changing his depreciation method each year to give the highest profit. Name the principle this would break and explain why he should not do this.
parts.answer: Consistency. Profits of different years could not be compared fairly, because changes in profit would be caused by the change of method, not by performance.

stem: Ming's shop has inventory at a cost of $12,000 and shop fittings with a carrying amount of $18,000. Ming has decided to close the shop next month. In a closing-down sale the inventory is expected to raise only $7,500 and the fittings $9,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the accounting principle that no longer applies to Ming's shop.
parts.answer: Going concern

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total value at which these assets should now be shown, and the reduction compared with their book values.
parts.answer: $16,500; a reduction of $13,500

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the fittings were previously shown at their carrying amount rather than at their sale value.
parts.answer: While the business was expected to continue (going concern), the fittings were to be used in the business, not sold, so they were shown at cost less depreciation; sale values were not relevant.
parts.working: 1 mark: business expected to continue/assets held for use. 1 mark: shown at cost less depreciation (historic cost), not sale value.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A small taxi business with total assets of $30,000 and a large airline both buy a set of spanners for $400. Explain why the taxi business might treat the spanners as a non-current asset while the airline treats them as an expense.
parts.answer: Materiality depends on the size of the business. $400 is a significant amount for the small taxi business, so it may be capitalised and depreciated. For the airline $400 is immaterial, so it is simply charged as an expense because the treatment would not affect users' decisions.
parts.working: 1 mark: materiality named/explained. 1 mark: significant for small business. 1 mark: insignificant for large business, so expensed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one other factor, apart from the amount, that can make an item material.
parts.answer: Its nature, e.g. an item that is unusual, illegal or of special interest to users (such as payments to directors).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Aliya bought a second-hand delivery van for $12,000 at an auction. The same model normally sells for $15,000. State the value at which the van will first be recorded in the books and name the principle applied.
parts.answer: $12,000; historic cost
parts.working: 1 mark: $12,000 (the price actually paid). 1 mark: historic cost.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of applying this principle.
parts.answer: Advantage: the cost is objective and can be checked against documents such as the invoice (reliable). Disadvantage: the recorded value may not show what the asset is worth now (e.g. it may be below market value or become out of date), so the statement of financial position may not show current values.

stem:
Bushra's draft profit for the year was $36,250. Her accountant found the following:
1 Bushra's private holiday costing $2,800 had been paid from the business bank account and debited to general expenses.
2 Electricity of $430 owing at the year end had not been recorded.
3 Closing inventory included goods valued at their cost of $1,600; they can now be sold for only $950.
4 An order of $3,000 for goods to be delivered next year had been recorded as a credit sale. The goods are included in closing inventory at cost.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit for the year.
parts.working: 36250 + 2,800 − 430 − 650 − 3,000 = 34970. 1 mark for each correct adjustment (max 3), 1 for the final figure.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the accounting principle that applies to each of items 1 to 4.
parts.answer: 1 business entity 2 matching (accruals) 3 prudence 4 realisation

author: HomiLabs

stem: At the year end Gareth's trade receivables were $24,600. He decided to maintain a provision for doubtful debts of 3% of trade receivables. The provision brought forward from last year was $600.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the provision for doubtful debts at the year end.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the amount charged in the income statement for the year.
parts.working: Increase only: 738 − 600 = 138. (Charging the whole provision loses the A mark.)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the net trade receivables shown in the statement of financial position.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Name the principle applied when making this provision and explain why it is made even though no customer has yet failed to pay.
parts.answer: Prudence. Some customers are likely not to pay, so the expected loss is recognised now and trade receivables are not overstated.
parts.working: 1 mark: prudence. 1 mark: avoids overstating assets/profit by recognising likely losses.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Zubair owns a factory building that cost $120,000 and is shown in his statement of financial position at that amount. He wants to show the building at its estimated market value of $300,000 because he is applying for a bank loan. Name the principle that requires the building to be shown at $120,000.
parts.answer: Historic cost

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise Zubair whether he should show the building at its market value. Justify your answer by giving two points for and two points against.
parts.answer: For: the statement of financial position would show a more up-to-date value; the bank would see a larger asset available as security; his net assets and capital would look stronger. Against: market value is an estimate and is subjective, so less reliable; it breaks the historic cost (and prudence) principle; an unrealised gain would be included; the bank will probably arrange its own valuation anyway; comparison with earlier years is distorted. Recommendation, e.g. he should keep the building at cost and give the bank a separate professional valuation.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for points for, up to 2 for points against, 1 for a justified recommendation (only if both sides are given).

stem: Kamal's draft profit for the year was $22,900. His capital on 1 January was $50,000 and drawings recorded were $9,000. Both amounts had been debited to business expense accounts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the corrected profit for the year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the corrected drawings.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate Kamal's closing capital before and after the corrections, and explain the result.
parts.answer: Both $63,900. Profit and drawings both increase by $2,340, so capital is unchanged.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Name the principle that has been broken.
parts.answer: Business entity

stem:
Hyun-woo's financial year ends on 31 December. During the year:
• wages paid were $31,200; this included $1,400 owing from the previous year, and $1,750 was owing at 31 December
• on 1 January rent of $9,900 was paid for the 15 months to 31 March of the following year

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the wages expense for the year.

parts.label: b

parts.text: Hyun-woo had charged the amounts paid ($31,200 and $9,900) as expenses. Calculate the effect of this on his profit for the year.
parts.answer: Profit was understated by $1,630.

parts.label: d

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A business changes its depreciation method every year so that profit stays about the same.
parts.answer: Consistency: use the same method each year unless a change gives a fairer view.
parts.working: 1 mark for the principle, 1 mark for the correct treatment.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Unsold inventory is valued at its selling price.
parts.answer: Prudence (also accept realisation): value at the lower of cost and net realisable value.
parts.working: 1 mark for the principle, 1 mark for the correct treatment.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The owner's private car insurance is charged as a business expense.
parts.answer: Business entity: treat it as drawings.
parts.working: 1 mark for the principle, 1 mark for the correct treatment.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The owner records the experience of her staff as an asset worth $50,000.

parts.working: 1 mark for the principle, 1 mark for the correct treatment.

author: HomiLabs
stem: For each treatment, name the accounting principle that has NOT been followed and state the correct treatment.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The owner of a business wants to compare this year's financial statements with last year's and with those of a similar business. Which quality of financial information is most important for this?
A comparability
B understandability
C materiality
D realisation
parts.answer: A comparability
parts.working: Comparability means information is prepared on the same basis over time and between businesses. Understandability (B) is about information being clear to users, not about comparisons. Materiality and realisation are principles, not qualities of information.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the main purpose of international accounting standards?
A to fix the selling prices that businesses may charge
B to reduce differences in accounting methods so that financial statements can be compared across countries
C to make sure every business makes a profit
D to replace the need for bank reconciliation statements
parts.answer: B to reduce differences in accounting methods so that financial statements can be compared across countries
parts.working: International accounting standards set out how items should be recognised, measured and presented, so that financial statements prepared in different countries are consistent and comparable. They do not guarantee a profit (C) or set prices.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by the relevance of financial information.
parts.answer: Information is relevant if it can influence users' decisions, for example by helping them assess past performance or predict future results, and it is available in time to be useful.
parts.working: 1 mark: affects/helps users' decisions. 1 mark: development (timely, helps predict or confirm).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is meant by the reliability of financial information.
parts.answer: Information is reliable if it is free from significant error and bias, can be checked (verified) and faithfully represents what it claims to show.
parts.working: 1 mark: free from error/bias. 1 mark: verifiable/faithful representation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why financial statements should be understandable. Give an example of how this can be achieved.
parts.answer: Users with reasonable knowledge of business must be able to make sense of the information; e.g. items are grouped under clear headings (non-current assets, current liabilities) and similar items are combined rather than listed in detail.
parts.working: 1 mark: users must be able to understand it to use it. 1 mark: example (clear headings, standard layout, notes).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Apart from understandability, name two other objectives a business should consider when selecting its accounting policies.
parts.answer: Any two of: comparability, relevance, reliability.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An investor is comparing the financial statements of a company in Pakistan with those of a similar company in Malaysia. Explain how international accounting standards help the investor.
parts.answer: Both companies follow the same rules for recognising and measuring items (e.g. inventory, depreciation), so their profits and assets are prepared on a similar basis and can be compared fairly when deciding where to invest.
parts.working: 1 mark: common rules/methods. 1 mark: makes the comparison meaningful for a decision.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why there may be a conflict between making information relevant and making it reliable. Give an example.
parts.answer: Relevant information must be up to date and available quickly, but checking it fully to make it reliable takes time. For example, a current market value of a building is more relevant than its cost but is an estimate, so it is less reliable; historic cost is reliable but may be out of date.
parts.working: 1 mark: relevance needs timeliness/current values. 1 mark: reliability needs checking/verifiable figures, which may be older. 1 mark: suitable example.

subtopic: Cash book and petty cash book

stem:
Zubair owns a building materials business. Ratios for two years:

stem: Saima sells kitchen appliances for cash only. Revenue is $180,000 a year with a gross margin of 30%. If she offers 30 days' credit, she expects extra sales of $60,000 a year at the same margin. She estimates irrecoverable debts at 2% of the extra sales and extra administration costs of $3,000 a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the expected increase in profit for the year if Saima offers credit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise Saima whether she should start selling on credit. Justify your answer by giving two points for and two points against.

Against: cash is received later, may need an overdraft; risk of irrecoverable debts may be higher than 2%; extra book-keeping and credit control work; estimates may not be achieved. Recommendation consistent with the points, e.g. offer credit with credit limits and checks.
parts.working: B1 each for two points for (max 2), B1 each for two points against (max 2), B1 recommendation.
