stem: Asma runs a bakery in Faisalabad and wants to buy a new oven costing $25,000. She can take a five-year bank loan at 9% interest per year, or use her personal savings, which earn 6% interest per year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State one advantage and one disadvantage of using a bank loan.
parts.answer: Advantage (any one): Asma keeps her savings for personal needs or emergencies; the cost is spread over five years; she still earns 6% on her savings. Disadvantage (any one): interest of 9% must be paid every year, reducing profit; repayments are needed even in poor years; the bank may require security.

parts.label: b

parts.answer: Loan: interest 9% × 25,000 = 2,250 a year reduces profit; increases liabilities. Savings: no interest, but she loses the 6% (1,500 a year) savings interest and has less personal cash for emergencies. Using savings is cheaper by $750 a year; reasoned recommendation either way.
parts.working: B1 cost of loan. B1 opportunity cost of savings. B1 a further relevant point (risk, liquidity, control). B1 recommendation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two possible effects of this on the business.
parts.answer: Any two: less cash available / liquidity problems; may need an overdraft and pay interest; greater risk of irrecoverable debts; may pay its own suppliers late and lose discounts.

stem: Mustafa's wholesale business pays its suppliers on average in 25 days but collects from its customers on average in 60 days.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why this situation may cause problems for the business.
parts.answer: Cash leaves the business after 25 days but comes in only after 60 days, so it must finance 35 days of trade; it may run short of cash or need an overdraft.
parts.working: B1 comparison of the periods. B1 consequence for cash.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one way to increase the trade payables payment period without upsetting suppliers.
parts.answer: Negotiate longer credit terms with suppliers (or find suppliers offering longer credit)

parts.label: c

parts.answer: Loss of cash discounts / damaged reputation / suppliers may refuse credit

stem: Aliya is a sole trader who runs a catering business. She plans a large expansion financed partly by friends who would invest but do not want to manage the business. She worries about losing her house if the expansion fails.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two advantages to Aliya of converting the business into a private limited company.
parts.answer: Any two: limited liability for shareholders; easier to raise capital by issuing shares; separate legal entity / continuity; may improve status with suppliers and banks.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two disadvantages of converting.
parts.answer: Any two: formation costs; accounts must follow legal requirements and may need audit; financial statements are less private; profits shared with other shareholders; some loss of control.

parts.label: c

parts.answer: A clear decision that follows from the points, e.g. yes, because the expansion is risky and limited liability protects her house.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the current ratio and liquid ratio for each shop. Give answers to two decimal places.
parts.answer: Shop P: current 2.40 : 1, liquid 0.93 : 1. Shop Q: current 2.00 : 1, liquid 1.36 : 1

parts.label: b

stem: Bashir's furniture business normally has revenue of $200,000 and cost of sales of $140,000 a year (gross margin 30%). A hotel offers to buy furniture with a normal selling price of $40,000 if Bashir gives a 10% discount. Cost of sales for this furniture would be at the normal rate (70% of normal selling price).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the gross profit on the special order.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the new overall gross margin if the order is accepted. Give your answer to two decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise Bashir whether he should accept the order. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: For: gross profit rises by $8,000; uses spare capacity; possible repeat business. Against: margin falls; regular customers may demand the same discount; may need extra expenses or credit risk. Recommendation.

parts.text: State two reasons why a business's gross margin may increase.

parts.label: b

parts.text:

B return on capital employed
C liquid (acid test) ratio

parts.answer: C liquid (acid test) ratio

stem: Imtiaz owns a pharmacy in Hyderabad and wants to compare its ratios with those of a pharmacy owned by his cousin in Karachi.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two users of a sole trader's financial statements, other than the owner, and state what each would want to know.
parts.answer: Any two, with a matching interest: bank/lender (ability to repay loan and interest); trade payables (ability to pay on time); employees (job security, ability to pay wages); tax authorities (profit for tax); potential buyer or partner (profitability).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State three limitations of comparing the ratios of two businesses.
parts.answer: Any three: different accounting policies (e.g. depreciation methods, inventory valuation); different sizes or locations; financial statements are historical; figures may be at different dates or for different periods; non-financial factors (staff, reputation) are ignored; one business may own premises and the other rent.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the main purpose of book-keeping?
A to record the financial transactions of a business accurately and in detail
B to interpret the financial statements and advise the owner
C to compare the results of the business with those of competitors
D to decide the selling prices of the goods the business sells
parts.answer: A to record the financial transactions of a business accurately and in detail
parts.working: Book-keeping is the detailed day-to-day recording of transactions. B and C are accounting (analysis and interpretation) tasks that use the book-keeping records; D is a management decision.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
During the year a florist's income was $68,200 and her expenses were $71,900. What was the result for the year and its effect on her capital?
A profit of $3,700; capital increases
B loss of $3,700; capital decreases
C loss of $3,700; capital increases
D profit of $3,700; capital decreases
parts.answer: B loss of $3,700; capital decreases
parts.working: Expenses exceed income: 71,900 − 68,200 = 3,700 loss. A loss reduces the owner's capital. A treats the difference as a profit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by income of a business.
parts.answer: Money earned (or to be received) by the business from its trading or other activities, e.g. sales, fees, rent received, commission received.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what is meant by an expense of a business.
parts.answer: A cost of running the business which is used up in earning income during the period, e.g. wages, rent, electricity.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Bilal drives a taxi in Quetta as a sole trader. Give one example of income and two examples of expenses of his business.
parts.answer: Income: fares received from passengers. Expenses (any two): fuel, vehicle repairs and servicing, vehicle insurance, licence fees, mobile phone bill, depreciation of the taxi.
parts.working: B1 income; 1 mark each for any two expenses. Do not accept buying the taxi (capital expenditure) or drawings.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Ayesha runs a beauty salon in Karachi. For each item state whether it is income, an expense or neither.
(i) fees received from customers
(ii) wages paid to an assistant
(iii) $5,000 paid in by the owner from her savings
(iv) $300 taken from the till by the owner for her own use
(v) a bank loan of $8,000 received
(vi) commission received for selling a supplier's products
parts.answer: (i) income; (ii) expense; (iii) neither (capital introduced); (iv) neither (drawings); (v) neither (a liability); (vi) income
parts.working: 1 mark each. Capital introduced, drawings and a loan change capital or liabilities but are not income or expenses.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a business owner needs records of the amounts owed by credit customers.
parts.answer: So that the owner knows how much each customer owes and when it is due (B1), and can send statements / chase late payers and decide whether to give more credit (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a business owner needs records of the amounts owed to suppliers.
parts.answer: So that the owner knows how much is owed and when it must be paid (B1), so that bills are paid on time, cash discounts are not lost and good relations / credit terms with suppliers are kept (B1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one other item of information a business owner can obtain from accounting records.
parts.answer: Any one: profit or loss for a period; value of assets; amount of liabilities; capital; bank/cash balance; inventory held; total sales or expenses.

stem:
Omar runs a mobile car wash in Dubai. His records for May show:
Washing fees received $6,840
Capital introduced by Omar $2,500
Bank loan received $4,000
Cleaning materials used $920
Wages of a helper $1,750
Fuel for the van $610
Omar's drawings $1,400
Insurance for the month $180

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Omar's profit for May.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the capital introduced, the bank loan and the drawings were not used in your calculation.
parts.answer: Capital introduced and the loan are money put into the business, not earned by it, so they are not income (B1); the loan is a liability that must be repaid (B1); drawings are taken by the owner for private use, not costs of running the business, so they are not expenses (B1).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Kiran owns a grocery shop and suspects that cash is going missing. Explain two ways in which keeping full accounting records could help her.
parts.answer: Any two, explained: (1) daily takings recorded and compared with cash counted/banked, so shortages are seen quickly; (2) records show who handled each transaction, so responsibility can be traced; (3) inventory records compared with sales show goods missing; (4) bank statements can be checked against the cash book (bank reconciliation) to spot unrecorded or missing amounts.
parts.working: 1 mark for each way, 1 mark for development (2 × 2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two other reasons why Kiran should keep accounting records.
parts.answer: Any two: to calculate profit or loss; to know assets and liabilities; to know amounts owed by and to her; to support a loan application; for tax purposes; to help planning and decisions.

stem: Oluwaseun makes leather bags in Lagos. His accounting records show that each bag costs $14.50 for materials and $9 for labour, and that a share of $4.25 of the workshop overheads should be added to each bag. He sells each bag for $40.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total cost of making one bag.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit on one bag.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the total profit if 320 bags are sold in the month.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain how accounting records helped Oluwaseun to set his selling price.
parts.answer: Records show the actual costs of materials, labour and overheads (B1), so he can set a price that covers all costs and gives the profit he wants; without them he might price below cost and make a loss (B1).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Mei Ling runs a fitness studio in Kuala Lumpur. Her accounting records show:
April: income $18,400, expenses $15,350
May: income $21,900, expenses $19,780
June: income $19,600, expenses $15,890

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit for each month.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the expenses of each month as a percentage of income. Give your answers correct to two decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State which month was the most successful. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: June: highest profit ($3,710) and the lowest share of income spent on expenses (81.07%), although May had the highest income.
parts.working: B1 month; B1 justification using profit/percentage (not income alone).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Mei Ling plans to employ an assistant at $2,200 a month. Using your answers, advise her whether she can afford to do this. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: New profits would be April $850, May −$80 (a loss) and June $1,510. April and June stay profitable, but in May the business would make a small loss and leave nothing for her own drawings. Advice either way accepted if justified, e.g. employ the assistant only if the extra help increases income (more classes) by at least $2,200 a month, or employ part-time.
parts.working: B1 new profit figures (850, −80, 1,510); B1 point for (two months still profitable / total profit still positive); B1 point against (May becomes a loss); B1 reasoned decision.

stem:
Tariq started a wholesale business on 1 January with money in the bank and no other assets. All transactions went through the bank. During the year:
• Sales $84,000, of which $9,600 was still owed by credit customers at the year end
• Purchases of goods $52,000, all paid; inventory unsold at the year end cost $7,500
• Expenses paid $18,300 (none owing or prepaid)
• Drawings $12,000
• Equipment bought $6,000 (ignore depreciation)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Tariq's profit for the year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the change in the bank balance during the year. State whether it is an increase or a decrease.
parts.answer: $13,900 decrease

parts.label: c
parts.text: Tariq says: 'The business made a profit, so the bank balance must have gone up.' Explain why he is wrong, using three items from the information.
parts.answer: Any three: credit customers still owe $9,600, counted as sales but not yet received; unsold inventory of $7,500 was paid for but is not an expense; the equipment of $6,000 reduced the bank but is not an expense (capital expenditure); drawings of $12,000 reduced the bank but are not an expense.

stem: Zara sells school uniforms from a market stall in Lahore. She records her cash takings and payments in a notebook only. Three schools have now asked to buy uniforms on 30 days' credit, and she wants to borrow from a bank to rent a small shop.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two benefits to Zara of keeping a full double-entry book-keeping system.
parts.answer: Any two: accurate profit figure; records of amounts owed by schools and to suppliers; arithmetical check through a trial balance; information for a bank loan application; easier control of cash and inventory; complete records for tax.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Advise Zara whether she should change from her notebook to a full double-entry system. Justify your answer by giving two points for and two points against.
parts.answer: For (any two): she now sells on credit to schools, so she needs receivables records; the business is growing, so errors are more likely; a bank will want proper statements before lending; she can measure profit accurately and control costs. Against (any two): takes time she could spend selling; she may need to pay a book-keeper or buy software; she may lack the skills; cost may be high for a small business. Decision: e.g. yes, because credit sales and growth make accurate records essential.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two points for and two against (4); 1 mark for a justified decision.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A business has total assets of $91,250 and capital of $63,700. Its only liabilities are trade payables of $9,300 and a bank loan. What is the bank loan?
A $18,250
B $27,550
C $36,850
D $81,950
parts.working: Total liabilities = assets − capital = 91,250 − 63,700 = 27,550; bank loan = 27,550 − 9,300 = 18,250. B is total liabilities (trade payables not deducted); C adds the payables; D ignores capital (91,250 − 9,300).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
On 1 March a trader's capital was $40,000. During March the business made a profit of $6,500, the owner took goods costing $800 for his family and he paid $3,000 of his own money into the business bank account. What was the capital on 31 March?
A $50,300
B $48,700
C $45,700

parts.working: 40,000 + 6,500 − 800 + 3,000 = 48,700. Goods taken are drawings and reduce capital; A adds them. C ignores the capital introduced.

parts.text: State the effect on total assets and total liabilities if the computer had been bought on credit.

stem: At 31 December the flower shop owned by Ji-woo in Busan had total assets of $57,340 and total liabilities of $18,925.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Rubina, the owner of a textile shop, paid her home electricity bill of $240 from the business bank account. State the effect of this on the business's assets, liabilities and capital.
parts.answer: Assets: bank decreases by $240 (B1). Liabilities: no change (B1). Capital: decreases by $240 because it is drawings (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this payment must not be recorded as an expense of the business.
parts.answer: The bill is for Rubina's private use, not for running the business (B1); the business and the owner are treated as separate, so it is drawings; treating it as an expense would understate profit (B1).

parts.text:
Each line shows the two effects of one transaction on the accounting equation. Suggest a transaction that would cause each.

(iii) Assets −$1,500; Liabilities −$1,500

parts.label: a
parts.text: A business buys a van costing $18,000. It pays $6,000 by bank transfer and the rest is financed by a loan from the van dealer. Calculate the change in (i) total assets and (ii) total liabilities.
parts.answer: (i) Assets increase by $12,000: van +18,000, bank −6,000. (ii) Liabilities increase by $12,000 (loan).

parts.text: State the effect of the transaction on capital. Explain your answer.

stem: Rashid's tyre business. Opening capital $29,000; profit for the year $13,450; drawings $7,600. At the year end: Machinery $32,000; Inventory $11,400; Trade receivables $5,300; Bank $2,850; Trade payables $6,700; Loan $10,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the capital at the end of the year using: opening capital + profit − drawings.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the capital at the end of the year using: assets − liabilities.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why both methods give the same answer.
parts.answer: Both measure the amount the business owes to the owner (B1); profit adds to net assets and drawings take resources out, so the change in capital equals the change in assets − liabilities (B1).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
On 1 October Joseph's hardware business in Kampala had: bank $9,000, inventory $6,000, equipment $12,000, trade payables $2,500 and a loan $5,000. During October:
1 Sold goods which had cost $2,000 for $1,700, received by bank transfer.
2 Paid loan interest of $250 by bank transfer.
3 Joseph took goods costing $400 for his own use.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the capital on 1 October.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the balance of each asset and each liability at the end of October.

author: HomiLabs

stem: During the year the total assets of Leila's printing business increased by $14,600 and its total liabilities decreased by $3,200. Her profit for the year was $21,900 and she paid in additional capital of $7,500.

parts.text: Calculate the increase in Leila's capital during the year.

parts.text: Explain why a reduction in liabilities increases the capital of the business when total assets do not change.

stem: Sophia's bakery in Athens: non-current assets $64,000; current assets $21,800; current liabilities $9,450; non-current liabilities $18,000.

parts.text: Calculate the net assets of the business.

parts.text: State the capital of the business. Explain why it equals the net assets.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The following year the business makes a loss of $6,200 and there are no drawings or capital introduced. Calculate the new capital and explain why the net assets must also fall by the same amount.
parts.answer: $52,150. A loss means expenses were greater than income, so more resources (e.g. bank) were used up or more liabilities incurred than income brought in; net assets fall by $6,200, matching the fall in capital.

parts.text: State the effect of transaction 1 on total assets, total liabilities and capital, giving amounts.

stem: Priya runs a dance school in Chennai. On 1 April her business had assets of $38,500 and liabilities of $9,200. For the year to 31 March, income was $27,400, expenses were $19,650 and drawings were $5,100. On 31 March liabilities were $11,050.

How is interest on partners' drawings treated in a partnership appropriation account?
A added to the profit for the year

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between a partner's capital account and a partner's current account.
parts.answer: The capital account records the long-term (fixed) capital the partner has invested, which changes only if capital is introduced or withdrawn (B1); the current account records the partner's share of profit, interest on capital, salary, drawings and interest on drawings each year (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two items which are credited to a partner's current account.
parts.answer: Any two: interest on capital; partner's salary; share of residual profit; (opening credit balance).

parts.answer: Any two: drawings (cash or goods); interest on drawings; share of residual loss; (opening debit balance).

stem:
Fatima and Gul are partners in a catering business in Islamabad. Fatima works full-time; Gul works part-time. They are discussing two options for sharing profits:
Option 1: Fatima receives a salary of $8,000 and the rest is shared equally.
Option 2: no salary; profits shared Fatima 60% and Gul 40%.
The profit for next year is expected to be $64,000. Ignore interest on capital and drawings.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Fatima's total share of profit under each option.
parts.answer: Option 1 $36,000; option 2 $38,400

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit for the year at which both options would give Fatima the same amount.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Advise Fatima which option to choose. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: At the expected profit of $64,000 Option 2 gives Fatima more ($38,400 v $36,000). Option 1 is better for her only if profit falls below $40,000, because the $8,000 salary is received first whatever the profit, so it is safer. Advice: choose Option 2 if she is confident profit will stay well above $40,000; choose Option 1 if profits are uncertain, since it guarantees a reward for her full-time work.
parts.working: B1 compares amounts at $64,000; B1 salary guaranteed/less risk; B1 uses the $40,000 break-even point; B1 justified decision.

stem: Hamza and Jamil share profits equally in a furniture partnership in Sialkot. Profit is $60,000 a year. Against (any two): profit shared three ways; the expected increase of $36,000 is only a forecast, close to the $30,000 needed; decisions need agreement of more partners; possible disagreements; each partner has unlimited liability for the others' business actions. Justified decision either way.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two for and two against; 1 mark for a justified decision.

stem:
Samuel runs a repair workshop in Nairobi and keeps no double-entry records.

In March Samuel brought his private van, valued at $9,000, into the business. He took $1,100 cash from the business each month for personal use.

parts.text: Calculate Samuel's capital on 1 January and on 31 December.
parts.answer: 1 January $27,100; 31 December $34,100
parts.working: Opening: 29,400 − 2,300 = 27,100 (B1). Closing: assets 43,300 (M1) − liabilities 9,200 (overdraft, suppliers, loan) = 34,100 (A1).

parts.label: b

parts.label: c

Against: costs time or money (book-keeper or software); the business is small and the capital comparison already gives a profit figure. Decision justified, e.g. yes, because he now has a loan and an overdraft and needs detailed figures to manage cash.
parts.working: B1 point for; B1 point against; B1 justified decision.

parts.text: Explain why this makes comparison with a business which bought similar premises recently less reliable.
parts.answer: The other business shows its premises at a much higher cost (B1), so its capital employed is larger and its ROCE looks lower even if it performs as well; Zaid's assets are understated, making his ROCE look higher (B1).

stem: A bakery in Faisalabad asks its bank for a loan. Its statement of financial position shows: inventory $26,000; trade receivables $4,800; bank $1,200 in one account, but a bank overdraft of $3,500 on another; trade payables $17,500.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the current ratio and the liquid (acid test) ratio. Give answers correct to two decimal places.
parts.answer: Current ratio 1.52 : 1; liquid ratio 0.29 : 1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the bank manager may be concerned about lending to the bakery.
parts.answer: The liquid ratio is well below 1 : 1 (0.29), so the bakery cannot pay its current liabilities from liquid assets (B1); it already has an overdraft and depends on selling inventory (B1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two other pieces of information the bank manager would want before deciding.
parts.answer: Any two: profit trend / ROCE; cash flow forecast; what the loan is for; security (assets that can be charged); owner's other debts; repayment plan.

parts.text: Calculate for Kamran: (i) gross margin, (ii) profit margin, (iii) current ratio, (iv) trade receivables turnover in days (365-day year, all sales on credit; nearest whole day).

parts.text: Compare Kamran's results with the industry averages. Advise him on two actions he should take. Justify your answer.

parts.answer: Business A 15.00%; Business B 20.00%

parts.text: Rania will invest $50,000 and receive the same ROCE as the business she joins. Calculate her expected annual return from each.

parts.text: Advise Rania which business to invest in. Justify your answer, including two limitations of using these figures.

stem: Grace owns a cleaning business in Kampala as a sole trader and works full-time in it. Revenue $140,000; profit for the year $31,500. A similar cleaning company has a profit margin of 11.00% after paying a manager a salary of $18,000.

parts.label: a

parts.label: b

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the adjustment is needed before comparing the two businesses, and state which business is performing better.
parts.answer: A sole trader's own work is not charged as an expense (her reward is drawings/profit), while the company pays its manager a salary, which reduces its profit (B1). After adjusting, Grace's margin is 9.64% compared with 11.00% (B1), so the company performs better (B1).
